questions.question: What is the sliding window technique and when do you use it?
questions.title: Sliding Window Technique Java | Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: The **sliding window** technique maintains a contiguous subarray or substring that slides over the data. Instead of recomputing from scratch at each position, you **add the element entering and remove the element leaving**. This turns many **O(n^2)** brute-force solutions into **O(n)** for problems on contiguous subarrays or substrings.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you recognize the pattern for contiguous subarray/substring problems and can distinguish fixed-size from variable-size windows
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Recomputing the entire window sum or property from scratch at each position instead of maintaining a running state
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Distinguish fixed-size windows (constant k) from variable-size windows (expand/shrink on a condition) with concrete examples

sections.title: Sliding Window: A Pattern for Contiguous Subarray Problems
sections.content:
The **sliding window technique** efficiently processes contiguous subarrays or substrings. Rather than re-examining the whole range at each step, you maintain a **running state** (a sum, a frequency map, or a set) and update it incrementally as elements enter and leave the window.

The key insight: you adjust, you don't recalculate. To find the maximum sum of any 3 consecutive elements in 1000 elements, the brute-force way recomputes a 3-number sum ~998 times — O(n^2)-ish. Sliding window computes the first sum once, then each slide just **adds one new number and subtracts one old number** — O(n). Two variants show up constantly: **fixed-size windows** where the size k is given, and **variable-size windows** where the window grows or shrinks based on a condition like "at most K distinct characters".

sections.title: Sliding Window at a Glance
sections.content:
blue|Sliding window|~process contiguous spans|keep a running state|add entering, remove leaving|turns O(n^2) into O(n)
emerald|Fixed-size|~size k is given|one loop|slide by one each step|max sum of k elements
amber|Variable-size|~grows and shrinks|two pointers left + right|expand, then contract on a rule|longest substring problems
rose|Signals|~when to reach for it|contiguous, consecutive|substring, subarray|longest, shortest, sum of k

sections.title: Fixed-Size Sliding Window in Action
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Recomputing from scratch**: writing nested loops that re-sum the next k elements for every start index is O(n^2). The whole point is incremental update — add one, remove one.
- **Mixing fixed and variable templates**: for "longest substring with at most 2 distinct characters" you can't slide a window of size 2 — the answer might be much longer. Use expand/contract logic.
- **Off-by-one in window boundaries**: be explicit about whether the window is `[left, right)` or `[left, right]` and stick to it.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Contiguous only**: applies to consecutive subarrays/substrings, not arbitrary selection.
- **Incremental update**: keep a running state, add the entering element, remove the leaving one.
- **Fixed-size**: exact size k -> one loop, slide by one element each time.
- **Variable-size**: a condition -> two pointers that expand and contract.
- **O(n) time**: each element is processed at most twice (entering and leaving).
- **Signals**: "contiguous", "subarray", "substring", "longest", "shortest", "sum of k".

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: The sliding window technique is a way to efficiently process contiguous subarrays or substrings. Instead of recalculating everything for each position, you maintain a running state and update it incrementally. You add the new element coming into the window and remove the element leaving the window. This turns a nested loop solution that's O of n squared into a single pass that's O of n. There are two main types. Fixed-size windows are used when the problem gives you an exact size k, like find the maximum sum of any three consecutive elements. You compute the first window once, then slide by adding the next element and subtracting the first element of the previous window. Variable-size windows are for problems with conditions, like longest substring with at most K distinct characters. You use two pointers. The right pointer expands to add elements. When the condition breaks, the left pointer contracts to restore validity. You track the maximum or minimum window size you see. The key mistake freshers make is using nested loops to recompute each window from scratch. That's what you're trying to avoid. The whole point is incremental update. You'd use this pattern whenever you see the words contiguous, consecutive, subarray, or substring combined with optimization keywords like maximum, minimum, longest, or shortest. It shows up constantly in coding interviews because it's a clean way to demonstrate you understand how to optimize brute force solutions.

questions.question: How do you find the maximum sum subarray of size k?
questions.title: Maximum Sum Subarray Size K Java | Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: Compute the sum of the **first k elements** to seed the window, then **slide one step at a time** — add the entering element and subtract the leaving one — tracking the maximum. This runs in **O(n) time, O(1) space**, far better than the O(n^2) nested-loop approach.

interviewer_intent.testing: Can you implement the classic fixed-size sliding window with correct boundary handling and clear incremental update logic
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using nested loops to recompute the sum for every window position, giving O(n^2) instead of incremental update
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Use descriptive names like windowSum and maxSum, handle the initial window separately, and explain the slide operation

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Two phases**: compute the initial window `[0, k-1]`, then slide from k to n-1.
- **Incremental update**: each slide subtracts `arr[i-k]` and adds `arr[i]` in O(1).
- **O(n) time**: each element is added once and removed once.
- **O(1) space**: only `windowSum`, `maxSum`, and an index.
- **Boundary**: start the sliding loop at index k.
- **Initialize maxSum** to the first window sum, not 0.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: To find the maximum sum subarray of size k, I'd use the sliding window technique. First, I compute the sum of the first k elements to establish the initial window. That's my starting windowSum. I also set maxSum equal to that initial windowSum because the first window is a valid candidate. Then I slide the window across the rest of the array. Starting from index k, for each position i, I update the windowSum by subtracting the element that's leaving the window, which is arr at i minus k, and adding the element that's entering, which is arr at i. After each update, I check if the new windowSum is greater than maxSum and update maxSum if it is. By the time I reach the end of the array, maxSum holds the answer. This runs in O of n time because I touch each element exactly twice, once when it enters the window and once when it leaves. The space complexity is O of one because I only use a few variables. The key mistake to avoid is using nested loops where you recompute the sum from scratch for every window. That's O of n squared. The whole point of sliding window is incremental update. You're adjusting the previous sum, not recalculating it. This pattern works for any fixed-size window problem where you need a maximum, minimum, or average over exactly k consecutive elements.

sections.title: Build the mental model
sections.content:
A **fixed-size window** keeps a constant size K, always removing the leftmost element before adding a new right one.

A **variable-size window** expands the right pointer until a condition breaks, then shrinks from the left until valid again.

Fixed-size uses one loop; variable-size uses two pointers with **expand/contract** logic.

Recomputing the entire window sum or property from scratch at each position instead of maintaining a running state

sections.title: Fixed-Size Window Slide
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TB A[sum first k elements
maxSum = windowSum] --> B{for i = k..n} B --> C[windowSum += arr i
windowSum -= arr i-k] C --> D[maxSum = max maxSum, windowSum] D --> B B -- done --> Z[return maxSum] ```

sections.title: Fixed-Size Sliding Window Implementation
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Nested loops recomputing the sum**: looping start index then summing k elements is O(n^2). Slide and update the sum incrementally instead.
- **Off-by-one in the slide loop**: start the loop at `i = k` (the first window ended at `k-1`); the update is `arr[i] - arr[i-k]`.
- **Forgetting to initialize maxSum**: starting `maxSum` at 0 breaks for all-negative arrays. Initialize it to the first window sum.

questions.question: What is the difference between a fixed-size and variable-size sliding window?
questions.title: Fixed-Size vs Variable-Size Sliding Window
questions.direct_answer: A **fixed-size window** keeps a constant size K, always removing the leftmost element before adding a new right one. A **variable-size window** expands the right pointer until a condition breaks, then shrinks from the left until valid again. Fixed-size uses one loop; variable-size uses two pointers with **expand/contract** logic.

interviewer_intent.testing: Conceptual clarity on the two variants and the ability to recognize which applies from the problem's constraints
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Applying a fixed-size template to a variable-size problem, forcing a size when it should be dynamic
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give a concrete example for each and state the rule: a number for size -> fixed; a condition like at most K distinct -> variable

sections.title: Two Sliding Window Variants: Fixed vs Variable Size
sections.content:
The sliding window pattern has two variants based on whether the size is **predetermined** or **dynamic**. A **fixed-size window** has a constant size K given by the problem — the window always holds exactly K elements. You compute the first K, then slide by removing the leftmost element and adding the next on the right, in one simple loop.

A **variable-size window** has no fixed size — it grows and shrinks based on a validity condition. You use two pointers: `right` expands to explore, `left` contracts when the window becomes invalid (outer for-loop moves right, inner while-loop moves left). Both achieve O(n). The decision is simple: "size k" / "exactly k consecutive" -> fixed-size; "at most K distinct", "without repeating", "longest", "shortest" -> variable-size. Mixing them up forces a size when the problem needs flexibility.

sections.title: Choosing the Variant
sections.content:
blue|Fixed-size|~size k is given|window always k wide|one loop, slide by one|max sum of k elements
emerald|Variable-size|~a rule, not a size|two pointers expand + contract|grows, then shrinks to stay valid|longest substring problems
amber|Both are O(n)|~each element seen O(1) times|fixed: one pass|variable: enters and leaves once|the inner while never restarts
rose|How to choose|~read the wording|a number for size -> fixed|a condition to satisfy -> variable|longest / shortest -> variable

sections.title: Fixed-Size vs Variable-Size Sliding Window
sections.content:
| Aspect | Fixed-Size Window | Variable-Size Window |
|---|---|---|
| Window size | Constant K throughout | Changes based on a condition |
| Loop structure | One for loop from K to n | For loop (expand) + while loop (contract) |
| Pointers | Single index i, window is [i-K, i) | Two pointers left and right |
| Update operation | Remove arr[i-K], add arr[i] | Expand right++, contract left++ when invalid |
| Problem keywords | size k, exactly k elements | longest, shortest, at most K, without repeating |
| Time complexity | O(n) one pass | O(n), each element processed at most twice |

sections.title: Fixed-Size: constant window of k
Variable-Size: grows and shrinks to stay valid
When to Use Each Variant
sections.content:
Use **fixed-size** when the problem gives a size K and asks for an operation over all windows of that size — "max sum of any 3 consecutive elements" — the 3 is your K.

Use **variable-size** when the problem gives a constraint and asks for the longest or shortest span satisfying it — "longest substring with at most 2 distinct characters" — you don't know the answer length up front, so you expand until invalid, then shrink. If you're unsure, ask: does the problem give me a number for the window size, or a rule to check?

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Fixed-size indicator**: an explicit size k or "exactly k consecutive elements".
- **Variable-size indicator**: a condition (at most K, without repeating) + "longest"/"shortest".
- **Fixed mechanics**: one loop, remove `arr[i-K]`, add `arr[i]`, window always size K.
- **Variable mechanics**: two pointers, right expands, left contracts when invalid.
- **Both O(n)**: variable-size is still O(n) because each element enters and leaves at most once.
- **Decision rule**: a number -> fixed; a validity condition -> variable.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: The difference between fixed-size and variable-size sliding window is whether the window has a constant size or changes dynamically. In a fixed-size window, the problem tells you the exact size k, like find the maximum sum of any five consecutive elements. You compute the first window of five elements, then slide it across the array by removing the leftmost element and adding the next element on the right. The window always has exactly five elements. The loop structure is simple, one for loop starting at index k, and in each iteration you do windowSum equals windowSum minus arr at i minus k plus arr at i. It's O of n time. In a variable-size window, the problem gives you a condition, not a size. For example, find the longest substring with at most two distinct characters. You don't know the answer length in advance. You use two pointers, left and right. The right pointer expands to add elements to the window. When the condition breaks, like you now have three distinct characters, you shrink from the left until the condition is valid again. The window size changes throughout the process. The loop structure is a for loop that moves right, and inside it there's a while loop that moves left when needed. It's still O of n because each element is processed at most twice. The key mistake freshers make is using a fixed-size approach for a variable-size problem. If you see the words longest or shortest with a condition, or at most K, that's variable-size. If you see size k or exactly k elements, that's fixed-size.

questions.question: How do you find the longest substring without repeating characters?
questions.title: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters Java | Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: Use a **variable-size sliding window** with a `HashSet` tracking characters in the window. Expand `right` to add characters; on a duplicate, **shrink from the left** until it's gone. Track the maximum window size. This runs in **O(n)** time and **O(min(n, m))** space, where m is the alphabet size.

interviewer_intent.testing: Can you implement the variable-size sliding window with HashSet-based duplicate detection and proper expand/contract logic
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using nested loops to check every substring for duplicates, giving O(n^2) or O(n^3) instead of the two-pointer pattern
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention the HashMap optimization storing each character's last index, letting left jump directly past the previous occurrence

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Variable-size window**: expand (right++) when valid, contract (left++) when invalid.
- **HashSet for uniqueness**: `window.contains(c)` detects duplicates in O(1).
- **Expand in the for loop**, contract in the inner while loop.
- **O(n) time**: each character is added and removed at most once.
- **HashMap optimization**: store each character's last index and jump `left` directly past it.
- **Window size**: `right - left + 1`.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: To find the longest substring without repeating characters, I'd use a variable-size sliding window with a HashSet. I have two pointers, left and right, both starting at zero. The HashSet tracks the characters currently in the window between left and right. I move the right pointer forward through the string, adding each character to the set. Before adding, I check if the character is already in the set. If it is, that means I have a duplicate, so the window is invalid. I then enter a while loop that shrinks the window from the left. In each iteration, I remove the character at the left pointer from the set and move left forward. This continues until the duplicate is gone and the set no longer contains the character at right. Once the window is valid again, I add the character at right to the set and calculate the window size as right minus left plus one. I track the maximum window size I've seen and return it at the end. The time complexity is O of n because even though there's a while loop inside a for loop, each character enters the set once and leaves once. The worst case is two n operations. The space complexity is O of the alphabet size, which is at most one twenty eight for ASCII or twenty six for lowercase English. A more advanced optimization uses a HashMap to store the most recent index of each character. When you find a duplicate, instead of shrinking one character at a time, you can jump the left pointer directly to the position right after the previous occurrence.

sections.title: Build the mental model
sections.content:
A **fixed-size window** keeps a constant size K, always removing the leftmost element before adding a new right one.

A **variable-size window** expands the right pointer until a condition breaks, then shrinks from the left until valid again.

Fixed-size uses one loop; variable-size uses two pointers with **expand/contract** logic.

Recomputing the entire window sum or property from scratch at each position instead of maintaining a running state

sections.title: Window Expand / Contract
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TB A[left = 0, set empty
maxLen = 0] --> B{for right = 0..n} B --> C{set has s right ?} C -- yes --> D[remove s left
left++] D --> C C -- no --> E[add s right] E --> F[maxLen = max maxLen, right-left+1] F --> B B -- done --> Z[return maxLen] ```

sections.title: Variable-Size Window with HashSet
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Nested loops checking every substring**: generating all substrings and testing each is O(n^2) or O(n^3). Use two pointers in one pass.
- **Not removing characters when shrinking**: you must remove `s.charAt(left)` before incrementing `left`, otherwise the while loop never exits.
- **Wrong window size**: the window is `[left, right]` inclusive, so the size is `right - left + 1`, not `right - left`.

questions.question: How do you find all anagrams of a pattern in a string?
questions.title: Find All Anagrams in String Java | Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: Use a **fixed-size sliding window** equal to the pattern length, with **character-frequency arrays** for the window and the pattern. Slide one character at a time, updating frequencies; when the window's counts match the pattern's, an anagram starts at the current index. This runs in **O(n)** time using array comparison.

interviewer_intent.testing: Can you combine fixed-size sliding window with frequency counting and do efficient array-based equality checks
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Sorting each window substring to check for anagrams, giving O(n*k*log k) instead of using frequency arrays for O(1) comparison
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Use Arrays.equals on two int[26] arrays for O(1) comparison and explain the frequency update when sliding

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Frequency matching**: anagrams have identical character frequencies.
- **Fixed-size window**: the window length equals the pattern length.
- **int[26] array**: index by `c - 'a'` for O(1) frequency updates.
- **Arrays.equals**: comparing two `int[26]` is O(26) = O(1).
- **Incremental update**: decrement `text.charAt(i-k)`, increment `text.charAt(i)`.
- **Window start**: `i - k + 1` when a match is found.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: To find all anagrams of a pattern in a string, I'd use a fixed-size sliding window with frequency counting. First, I create two frequency arrays of size twenty six, one for the pattern and one for the current window. I build the pattern frequency array by iterating through the pattern and incrementing the count for each character. Then I initialize the window frequency array by processing the first k characters of the text, where k is the pattern length. After that, I compare the two arrays using Arrays dot equals. If they match, the first window is an anagram, so I add index zero to my result list. Then I slide the window across the rest of the text. At each position i starting from k, I update the window frequency by decrementing the count of the character leaving the window, which is at position i minus k, and incrementing the count of the character entering, which is at position i. After each update, I compare the two frequency arrays again. If they match, I add the start index of the current window to the result. The start index is i minus k plus one, not i. The time complexity is O of n because I touch each character a constant number of times. The comparison using Arrays dot equals is O of twenty six, which is O of one for a fixed alphabet. The key mistake to avoid is sorting each window substring to check for anagrams. That's O of n times k log k. Using frequency arrays with incremental updates is much faster and is the standard approach.

sections.title: Build the mental model
sections.content:
A **fixed-size window** keeps a constant size K, always removing the leftmost element before adding a new right one.

A **variable-size window** expands the right pointer until a condition breaks, then shrinks from the left until valid again.

Fixed-size uses one loop; variable-size uses two pointers with **expand/contract** logic.

Recomputing the entire window sum or property from scratch at each position instead of maintaining a running state

sections.title: Frequency Window Slide
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TB A[build patternFreq
build first windowFreq] --> B{freqs equal?} B -- yes --> S0[record index 0] B -- no --> C{for i = k..n} S0 --> C C --> D[windowFreq-- leaving char
windowFreq++ entering char] D --> E{freqs equal?} E -- yes --> F[record i-k+1] E -- no --> C F --> C C -- done --> Z[return result] ```

sections.title: Fixed-Size Window with Frequency Arrays
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Sorting each window**: extracting and sorting each substring is O(n * k log k). Use frequency arrays with O(1) comparison.
- **Incorrect window start index**: when a match is found at loop index i, the window starts at `i - k + 1`, not i.
- **Using a HashMap when an array suffices**: for lowercase letters, `int[26]` is faster and simpler than `HashMap<Character, Integer>`.

questions.question: How do you find the longest substring with at most K distinct characters?
questions.title: Longest Substring with At Most K Distinct Characters
questions.direct_answer: Use a **variable-size sliding window** with a `HashMap` of character frequencies. Expand `right` and add characters; when the map has **more than K** distinct keys, shrink from the left, decrementing counts and **removing a key when it hits zero**. Track the maximum window length. This runs in **O(n)** time.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can adapt the sliding window template to a distinct-character constraint and correctly manage map key removal
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Forgetting to remove the key from the map when its count drops to zero, causing incorrect distinct-character counts
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Call out the map-key-removal edge case explicitly and explain why each character is processed at most twice

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **HashMap for frequencies**: counts each character in the window.
- **Map size = distinct count**: must not exceed K.
- **Key removal on zero**: call `map.remove(c)` when a count drops to 0.
- **Expand in the for loop, contract in the while loop**.
- **O(n) time**: each character is added once and removed at most once.
- **Window size**: `right - left + 1`.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: To find the longest substring with at most K distinct characters, I'd use a variable-size sliding window with a HashMap. I have two pointers, left and right, both starting at zero. The HashMap tracks the frequency of each character in the current window. The number of keys in the map tells me how many distinct characters I have. I move the right pointer forward through the string, adding each character to the map and incrementing its count. After each addition, I check if the map size is greater than K. If it is, the window is invalid because I have too many distinct characters. I enter a while loop that shrinks the window from the left. In each iteration, I get the character at the left pointer, decrement its frequency in the map, and then check if the frequency is now zero. If it is, I must remove that key from the map entirely. This is crucial because if I leave a key with count zero in the map, the map size will be wrong. After removing zero-count keys, I increment the left pointer. This continues until the map size is less than or equal to K again. Once the window is valid, I calculate its size as right minus left plus one and update my maximum length if this window is larger. The time complexity is O of n because each character enters the map once and leaves at most once, even though there's a while loop inside the for loop. The key mistake to avoid is forgetting to remove the map key when its count drops to zero.

sections.title: Build the mental model
sections.content:
A **fixed-size window** keeps a constant size K, always removing the leftmost element before adding a new right one.

A **variable-size window** expands the right pointer until a condition breaks, then shrinks from the left until valid again.

Fixed-size uses one loop; variable-size uses two pointers with **expand/contract** logic.

Recomputing the entire window sum or property from scratch at each position instead of maintaining a running state

sections.title: Window with Distinct-Count Constraint
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TB A[left = 0, map empty
maxLen = 0] --> B{for right = 0..n} B --> C[map.put s right, count+1] C --> D{map.size > k?} D -- yes --> E[decrement s left
remove key if 0, left++] E --> D D -- no --> F[maxLen = max maxLen, right-left+1] F --> B B -- done --> Z[return maxLen] ```

sections.title: Variable-Size Window with HashMap and Key Removal
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Not removing zero-count keys**: decrementing to zero but leaving the key makes `map.size()` overcount distinct characters — remove the key when it hits zero.
- **Misreading map.size()**: it's the number of keys (distinct characters), not the sum of frequencies.
- **Shrinking too aggressively**: the while condition is `map.size() > k`, not `>= k`, or you shrink valid windows.

beats.text: Use a variable-size sliding window with a HashMap tracking character frequencies; expand right freely and shrink from the left whenever the number of distinct characters exceeds K.

items: Expand: add the right character and bump its count in the map.
Contract: while the map has more than K keys, decrement the left character, remove its key at zero, and advance left.

beats.text: gotcha: forgetting to remove the key from the map when its count drops to zero makes map.size() overcount, producing wrong answers.

items: Using map.size() while leaving stale zero-count keys in the map.
Shrinking on map.size() >= k instead of > k, which discards valid windows.
